chapters.title: Chapter 1: Pricing a Bond from Its Cash Flows

lessons.title: Anatomy of a Bond Cash Flow: Face Value, Coupon, Tenor, and Settlement

children.text: Every formula in this course, from yield to maturity to convexity, does one thing: it reads a list of future payments and turns it into a number. If you get that list wrong, every number built on it is wrong too. So before we price anything, we will take a real Government of India bond apart and write down exactly what it pays, when, and to whom. By the end of this lesson you will be able to look at any G-Sec, T-bill or NCD on RBI Retail Direct, NSE or BSE and build its cash flow schedule from scratch.

body.text: A bond is not a price on a screen. It is a schedule of promised cash flows. Price, yield, duration and convexity are simply different ways of reading that schedule.

children.text: The Four Numbers That Define Every Bond

markDefs.definition: The amount the issuer repays at maturity, and the base on which coupons are calculated. Also called par value or principal. ₹100 for G-Secs.
The fixed annual interest rate the issuer pays, expressed as a percentage of face value.
How many times a year the coupon is paid. Semi-annual (twice a year) for Government of India securities.
The date on which the final coupon and the face value are repaid and the bond ceases to exist.

children.text: Take the 7.18% GS 2033, one of the most actively traded Government of India securities. Its name already tells you most of what you need. Four numbers define its cash flows completely: the
face value
, the
coupon rate
, the
coupon frequency
and the
maturity date
. Nothing else, not the market price, not the rating, not today's RBI repo rate, changes what the bond will pay you.

stats.label: Coupon rate
stats.context: On face value, not on price

stats.label: Frequency
stats.context: ₹3.59 per unit, every 14 Feb and 14 Aug

body.text: Read a G-Sec name left to right: "7.18%" is the coupon rate, "GS" means Government Security issued by the Centre, and "2033" is the maturity year. A State Development Loan reads the same way, for example "7.45% Maharashtra SDL 2034". The exact maturity and coupon dates are listed on RBI Retail Direct and on the CCIL website.

body.latex: \text{Coupon per period} = \frac{\text{Face Value} \times \text{Coupon Rate}}{\text{Payments per Year}}
body.caption: 7.18% GS 2033: ₹100 × 7.18% ÷ 2 = ₹3.59 per unit, every six months.

body.title: Size one coupon
body.prompt: You hold 500 units of the 7.18% GS 2033, each with a face value of ₹100. How much do you receive on each coupon date?
body.explanation: Face value held = 500 × ₹100 = ₹50,000. Coupon per period = ₹50,000 × 7.18% ÷ 2 = ₹1,795. You receive this every 14 February and 14 August until maturity.

children.text: Building the Cash Flow Schedule

Kavita Iyer, a 41-year-old chartered accountant in Chennai, buys ₹1 lakh face value (1,000 units) of the 7.18% GS 2033 on RBI Retail Direct. Her trade settles on 15 September 2026. The August 2026 coupon has already been paid to the previous holder, so her first coupon is on 14 February 2027. From there, the schedule writes itself: ₹3,590 every six months, and on the final date, the last coupon plus her ₹1,00,000 back.

body.caption: Kavita's cash flows on ₹1 lakh face value of 7.18% GS 2033 (contractual dates; if a date is a holiday, payment moves to a working day)

children.text: Look at the shape of that chart. Thirteen small bars and one tower. Of the ₹1,50,260 Kavita will receive, ₹1,03,590 arrives on a single day, almost seven years away. That is not a quirk of this bond; it is true of every plain coupon bond, and it is the root of interest rate risk. When most of your money sits far in the future, a change in interest rates changes what that future money is worth today by a lot. Chapter 3 turns this observation into a precise number called duration.

body.label: Share of total cash arriving on the final date
body.context: ₹1,03,590 ÷ ₹1,50,260. The longer the bond and the lower the coupon, the higher this share.

children.text: Tenor vs Residual Maturity

markDefs.definition: The length of a bond's life from its issue date to its maturity date. Fixed at issue.
The time left from today (or from your settlement date) until maturity. Shrinks every day you hold the bond.

children.text: The 7.18% GS 2033 was issued in 2023 as a 10-year bond. That 10 years is its
original tenor
. But Kavita, settling in September 2026, holds a bond with a
residual maturity

of just under seven years. Only the residual maturity matters for pricing and risk. Traders on the NSE debt segment and bond desks at banks routinely call this bond "the old 10-year" once a newer benchmark is issued, precisely because its remaining life has shrunk.

columns.label: Original tenor
points: Measured from issue date to maturity date
Fixed forever once the bond is issued
Useful for describing the bond: "a 10-year G-Sec"
Irrelevant to what you pay or earn today

columns.label: Residual maturity
points: Measured from your settlement date to maturity date
Falls by one day every day
Decides how many coupons you will still receive
Drives the bond's price, yield and interest rate risk

body.title: Which maturity matters?
body.question: Two bonds on RBI Retail Direct both show a 7.2% coupon. Bond A is a 5-year G-Sec issued last month. Bond B is a 14-year G-Sec issued in 2017. Which bond has more cash flows still left to pay?
options: Bond A, because 5-year bonds are newer
Bond B, because its original tenor of 14 years is longer
Neither: Bond A has about 5 years left and Bond B about 5 years left, so both have roughly the same
It cannot be told without the market price
body.explanation: Bond B was issued in 2017 with a 14-year tenor, so it matures around 2031. Bond A, issued last month for 5 years, also matures around 2031. Their residual maturities are about the same, so they have roughly the same number of coupons left. Original tenor is a label; residual maturity decides the cash flows.

children.text: The Coupon Is Fixed on Face Value, Not on Price

This is the single most common mistake retail investors make with bonds. Suppose Kavita paid ₹104 per unit instead of ₹100. Her coupon does not rise to 7.18% of ₹104. It stays at ₹3.59 per unit every six months, because the coupon is always calculated on the ₹100 face value. On ₹104 invested, ₹7.18 a year works out to only 6.90%. And at maturity she gets back ₹100, not ₹104.
The price you pay changes your return; it never changes the cash flows.
That gap between the coupon rate and your actual return is exactly what yield to maturity measures, which is the subject of Chapter 2.

body.title: What is the coupon calculated on?
body.textWithBlank: A bond's coupon is always calculated on its ___ value, no matter what price you paid for it.
body.explanation: Coupons are a fixed percentage of face value (par). Buying at ₹104 or ₹96 does not change the ₹3.59 you receive every six months on each ₹100 unit of 7.18% GS 2033.

children.text: Not Every Bond Pays the Same Way
The Indian bond market offers three basic cash flow patterns, and you need to recognise each before you can price it.

body.caption: Common Indian fixed income instruments and how they pay

cells: Fixed coupon every six months, face value at maturity
RBI Retail Direct, NSE goBID, BSE Direct, brokers
Fixed coupon every six months, face value at maturity
No coupon; bought below ₹100, redeemed at ₹100
RBI Retail Direct, NSE goBID, BSE Direct
Choice of monthly, annual or cumulative payout
IPO window via Zerodha, Groww and other brokers, then NSE and BSE
Usually annual coupon, face value at maturity
NSE and BSE RFQ platforms, SEBI-registered online bond platforms

children.text: Zero-coupon: the Treasury bill

markDefs.definition: A bond that pays no periodic interest. It is issued below face value, and the entire return is the difference between the purchase price and the face value received at maturity.

children.text: A T-bill has exactly one cash flow: ₹100 at maturity. It is a
zero-coupon
instrument, so your entire return comes from buying it at a discount. If a 364-day T-bill is allotted at ₹93.50, you earn ₹6.50 on ₹93.50 over 364 days. RBI annualises this using a 365-day year.

body.title: Annualise a 91-day T-bill
body.prompt: A 91-day T-bill is allotted at ₹98.35 in an RBI auction. What is its annualised yield? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Gain = ₹100 − ₹98.35 = ₹1.65. Yield = (1.65 ÷ 98.35) × (365 ÷ 91) = 0.016777 × 4.010989 = 6.73% a year. Note that ₹1.65 on ₹100 would suggest 6.62%; dividing by the price you actually paid, not the face value, is what makes it 6.73%.

children.text: Payout choices: the public issue NCD

markDefs.definition: Non-convertible debenture: a corporate bond that cannot be converted into shares. Public issues are open to retail investors and listed on NSE and BSE after allotment.

children.text: When an NBFC launches a public
NCD

issue, the same ₹1,000 debenture usually comes in several series with different payout options. Consider an illustrative 3-year series at 9.50% a year, and an investor putting in ₹1 lakh (100 NCDs). The face value and rate are identical; only the timing of cash flows changes.

body.caption: ₹1 lakh in an illustrative 3-year, 9.50% NCD: annual vs cumulative series

children.text: The cumulative series pays ₹2,793 more in total because interest compounds inside the bond: ₹1,00,000 × 1.095 × 1.095 × 1.095 = ₹1,31,293. But the annual series hands you ₹19,000 two years earlier, which you could reinvest yourself. Which is better depends on what money received earlier is worth to you. That question, how much a rupee in the future is worth today, is the whole of the next lesson.
Settlement: When the Bond Actually Becomes Yours

markDefs.definition: The day the buy or sell order is executed and the price is agreed.
The day money and securities actually change hands. Ownership, and the right to future cash flows, passes on this date.
The cut-off date on which the issuer checks its register of holders. Whoever holds the bond on this date receives the next coupon.

children.text: Three dates decide who gets which cash flow. The
trade date
is when you click buy. The
settlement date

is when you pay and the bond lands in your RBI Retail Direct gilt account or your CDSL or NSDL demat account; for most secondary market trades in G-Secs and listed corporate bonds in India this is T+1. The
record date
is when the issuer freezes its list of holders for the next coupon. For listed corporate bonds and NCDs, SEBI's framework sets the record date 15 days before the coupon or redemption date.

body.title: Arjun's NCD sale around a coupon date (illustrative)

events.title: Record date
events.description: 15 days before the coupon date. Arjun is the registered holder of 200 NCDs, so he is entitled to the upcoming coupon.

events.title: Trade date
events.description: Arjun sells all 200 NCDs on the NSE debt segment. The bond is now trading ex-interest, so the buyer's price excludes the upcoming coupon.

events.title: Settlement date (T+1)
events.description: Sale proceeds reach Arjun's account and the NCDs move to the buyer's demat account.

events.title: Coupon date
events.description: The ₹19,000 annual coupon is credited to Arjun, not the buyer, because Arjun held the NCDs on the record date.

body.text: Buying a bond a few days before its coupon date does not mean you will receive that coupon. If you settle after the record date, the coupon goes to the seller, and the price you paid should already reflect that. Always check the record date on the exchange or the issuer's disclosures before buying close to a coupon date.

body.title: Build the schedule for Arjun's buyer
body.scenario: Sneha Rao, a software engineer in Bengaluru, buys Arjun's 200 NCDs on 15 March 2027 (settlement 16 March 2027). Each NCD has a face value of ₹1,000, pays a 9.50% coupon once a year on 25 March, and matures on 25 March 2029, when the final coupon and face value are repaid. The record date is 15 days before each payment date.
body.prompt: List every cash flow Sneha will receive, with dates and amounts, and explain why the 25 March 2027 coupon is missing from her list.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Face value held: 200 × ₹1,000 = ₹2,00,000. Annual coupon: ₹2,00,000 × 9.50% = ₹19,000.
2. 25 March 2027: nothing for Sneha. She settled on 16 March, after the 10 March record date, so Arjun receives this coupon.
3. 25 March 2028: ₹19,000 coupon. Sneha is the holder on the record date (10 March 2028).
4. 25 March 2029: ₹19,000 final coupon plus ₹2,00,000 face value = ₹2,19,000.
5. Total cash Sneha will receive: ₹2,38,000. The price she paid on 15 March 2027 should have been lower than it would have been just before the record date, because the ₹19,000 coupon no longer comes with the bond.

body.title: Bonds whose cash flows are not fixed

children.text: This course focuses on fixed-coupon bonds, because they are the foundation for everything else. But you will meet these variations in the Indian market, and each changes the cash flow schedule:
Floating Rate Bonds (GOI FRBs):
the coupon resets every six months based on a benchmark such as the T-bill yield, so future coupon amounts are unknown today.
Callable bonds:
the issuer can repay early, typically when rates fall, which cuts off the remaining coupons. Many bank AT1 and Tier 2 bonds carry call options. Chapter 2 covers yield to call.
STRIPS:
a G-Sec split into separate zero-coupon pieces, one for each coupon and one for the principal, each traded on its own.
Amortising bonds:
principal is repaid in instalments over the bond's life rather than in one lump sum, common in some infrastructure and securitised debt.

body.label: RBI Retail Direct
body.description: RBI's platform for individuals to open a gilt account and buy G-Secs, SDLs and T-bills directly. Each security's page shows its coupon, maturity date and coupon dates.

body.title: Before you buy any bond, write down its cash flows
steps: Note the face value per unit: ₹100 for G-Secs and T-bills, ₹1,000 or ₹10,000 for most corporate bonds and NCDs.
Find the coupon rate and payment frequency, and calculate the rupee coupon per period on the face value you are buying.
Find the exact maturity date and the coupon dates, not just the maturity year.
Count the coupons remaining from your settlement date, not from the issue date.
Check the record date if you are buying within a few weeks of a coupon date.
Check for a call option, floating coupon or amortisation schedule that would change the cash flows.
List every date and amount in a spreadsheet. This is the input for every calculation in the rest of this course.

cards.definition: The amount repaid at maturity and the base for coupon calculations. ₹100 for G-Secs.
Annual interest as a percentage of face value. It never changes with the market price.
The bond's life from issue date to maturity date.
The time left from settlement to maturity. This is what matters for pricing and risk.
Pays no coupons; bought at a discount and redeemed at face value. T-bills are the Indian example.
When cash and securities change hands. T+1 for most secondary trades in Indian G-Secs and listed corporate bonds.
The date the issuer checks who holds the bond. That holder receives the next coupon.

points: A bond is a schedule of promised cash flows defined by four numbers: face value, coupon rate, frequency and maturity date.
Coupon per period = face value × coupon rate ÷ payments per year. For 7.18% GS 2033, ₹3.59 per ₹100 every six months.
The coupon is always on face value. Paying ₹104 instead of ₹100 changes your return, never the cash flows.
Residual maturity, not original tenor, decides how many cash flows remain and drives price and risk.
Most of a plain bond's cash arrives on the final date: 68.9% for Kavita's 7.18% GS 2033 holding. This is the root of interest rate risk.
T-bills pay one cash flow at maturity; NCDs can pay monthly, annually or cumulatively on the same face value.
Settlement is T+1 for most Indian bond trades, and whoever holds the bond on the record date gets the next coupon.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. The investors, NCD terms and T-bill prices shown are illustrative. Coupon dates, record dates, face values and settlement cycles can differ by security and may change with RBI and SEBI rules, so always verify the details on RBI Retail Direct, CCIL, NSE, BSE or the issue documents before investing, and consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser for decisions about your own portfolio.
